home.label: The learning salon
home.title: Less memorising. More discovering.
home.text: Unpack an algorithm, plan a lesson, meet computing pioneers and investigate myths. Tea is optional. Curiosity is welcome.
algorithm.title: Ada’s algorithm, step by step
algorithm.deck: Bernoulli numbers without the panic. Advance at your own pace and watch what happens to every fraction.
algorithm.heading: A program before the computer
algorithm.intro: In Note G, published in 1843, Ada described a calculation for Babbage’s proposed Analytical Engine. Her table showed how to calculate a Bernoulli number using earlier values.
algorithm.scope: This is a modern educational visualisation inspired by Note G. It uses a simple recurrence, not an exact simulation of the original machine’s cards and registers. Bernoulli numbers appear, for example, in formulas for sums of powers.
algorithm.notation: Ada’s B1, B3, B5 and B7 correspond to today’s B2, B4, B6 and B8. The original table calculated her B7, which is modern B8 = -1/30. Our modern convention uses B0 = 1 and B1 = -1/2.
algorithm.recipeTitle: A recipe without a steam boiler
algorithm.recipe1: Take the Bernoulli numbers you already know. For each term, find C(n+1, k), the number of ways to choose k elements from n+1.
algorithm.recipe2: Multiply each known number by its coefficient and add it to the running total S.
algorithm.recipe3: Reverse the sign of the total and divide by n+1. The result is the required Bn.
algorithm.joke: The fractions stay exact. The tea may be approximately warm.
algorithm.labTitle: A calculation under the magnifying glass
algorithm.instructions: Start with B2. Next step adds one term at a time. Go back, restart or choose a more demanding number. Nothing advances automatically.
algorithm.knownHint: These values are inputs to the current calculation. The highlighted term is the one being used.
algorithm.nojs: The interactive calculation needs JavaScript. Expand the worked B2 example below to read the complete calculation.
algorithm.workedText: The coefficients are 1 and 3. The total is -1/2. Reversing the sign and dividing by three gives 1/6.
algorithm.startText: We are looking for B{n}. Earlier values are already known and we begin with S = 0.
algorithm.addText: Multiply the coefficient {coefficient} by the value {value}. Add this term to the total. A zero term is still a valid part of the procedure.
algorithm.finishText: Reverse the sign of the total and divide by n+1. This gives an exact fraction without rounding.
teachers.title: Teachers’ corner
teachers.deck: One lesson, four activities and a classroom full of curiosity. Ready-to-use materials to bring Ada into today’s schools.
teachers.heading: 45 minutes with Ada
teachers.intro: For learners aged about 12 and above, and beginner programmers. No coding experience is needed; basic fraction skills help with the numerical activity.
teachers.materials: Bring paper, a pen and a device with a web browser. One device per pair or a teacher’s projector is enough. The downloaded worksheet also works offline.
teachers.goals: Explain an algorithm in their own words, follow a short sequence of instructions, distinguish fact from fiction and cite a source for a historical claim.
teachers.downloadText: The student worksheet and teacher solutions are available as PDF, Word (DOCX) and HTML in the current language. Choose the format that suits you.
teachers.printHelp: Download the PDFs and print them straight away. The HTML version opens in a browser and also works offline.
teachers.lesson1: Can you write a program for a machine that has not yet been completed? Let learners predict the answer before introducing Ada.
teachers.lesson2: In pairs, explore two claims in Facts and myths. Open a source and record the evidence supporting the answer.
teachers.lesson3: Build a short program in the simulator. Predict the result first, then run it. With a shared projector, learners can dictate the sequence of instructions.
teachers.lesson4: Follow the B2 calculation step by step. One learner reads the instruction while another records the total. For younger groups, replace fractions with the paper algorithm in activity 1.
teachers.lesson5: Use the existing quiz for revision. Everyone shares one new thing they learnt and one question they still want to answer.
teachers.q1: Start with 2. Add 3, multiply the result by 4 and subtract 1. Record every intermediate value. What changes if you swap the first two instructions?
teachers.a1: Original order: 2 → 5 → 20 → 19. After swapping addition and multiplication: 2 → 8 → 11 → 10. The order of instructions affects the result.
teachers.q2: Assess this claim: Ada ran her algorithm on a completed Analytical Engine. Find a reliable source, record its title and explain your verdict in one sentence.
teachers.a2: Myth. The Analytical Engine was not completed during Ada’s lifetime. A suitable source is Computer History Museum, Ada Lovelace, or the historical text and context in Sources.
teachers.q3: Use B0 = 1 and B1 = -1/2. Calculate S = 1 × B0 + 3 × B1, then B2 = -S / 3. Explain what a running total means.
teachers.a3: S = 1 - 3/2 = -1/2. B2 = -(-1/2) / 3 = 1/6. A running total stores the sum of the terms processed so far.
teachers.q4: In Punched cards, create a short program using the available instructions. Write down the expected result, run the program and change one instruction. Explain the difference. Without a device, use activity 1 instead.
teachers.a4: Open activity: assess the prediction, recorded instructions and explanation of the change. There is no single required result. Paper example: changing the final subtraction from 1 to 2 changes 19 to 18.
teachers.differentiate: Beginners can use whole numbers and dictate steps to a partner. Advanced learners can compare B4 with B2 and explain the coefficients. Allow written or spoken answers, larger text and work without a time limit.

pioneers.title: Women in computing history
pioneers.deck: From symbolic instructions to flight software. Four pioneers whose work helped change what computers could do.
pioneers.intro: Computing history was not made by one genius at a lonely desk. It is also a story of teams, collaboration and women whose work deserves attention.
pioneers.context: The connections to Ada below are thematic parallels. We do not claim that she directly inspired or personally influenced each of these scientists.
pioneers.connectionTitle: How this story connects to Ada
pioneers.hopper: Grace Hopper developed early compilers and FLOW-MATIC, a language that influenced COBOL. She helped bring programming closer to human language. COBOL was a collaboration between multiple people and organisations.
pioneers.hopperLink: Understandable symbols can represent precise instructions. The bridge between human intention and what a machine can execute matters.
pioneers.hamilton: Margaret Hamilton led the team developing flight software for the Apollo programme. Her work included reliability, testing and task priorities. Successful missions depended on many specialists working together.
pioneers.hamiltonLink: An idea for a calculation is not enough. We need a precise procedure and must consider what happens under unexpected conditions.
pioneers.bartik: Jean Bartik was one of the six original ENIAC programmers. She later helped convert it into a stored-program computer and also worked on BINAC and UNIVAC I.
pioneers.bartikLink: A mathematical problem must be broken into operations a machine can handle. Programming involves more than typing into an editor.
pioneers.allen: Frances Allen researched compiler optimisation and automatic parallel execution. Her work helped programs run more efficiently. She became the first woman to receive the Turing Award, for 2006.
pioneers.allenLink: The order and organisation of calculations affect performance. Good programming also means finding a more effective procedure.
pioneers.challenge: Choose one person. Use the linked source to find a specific project, collaborators and the problem she tackled. Write three sentences without using “the only one” or “all by herself”.
myths.title: Fact or myth?
myths.deck: A historical fog detector. Five claims, verifiable sources and a clear distinction between Ada’s words and our jokes.
myths.intro: Make a guess before revealing the explanation. In history, the most honest answer is sometimes “needs context”.
myths.a1: She is often described this way in connection with the procedure published in 1843. Her collaboration with Babbage and the originality of individual contributions remain subjects of historical discussion. The title is shorthand, not the whole story.
myths.q2: She only translated someone else’s article.
myths.a2: She added extensive notes to Menabrea’s article, including a computational procedure. Her published contribution therefore went beyond translation alone.
myths.q3: She ran her program on a completed Analytical Engine.
myths.a3: The Analytical Engine was not completed during her lifetime. The table in Note G described planned operations, not a record of a successful run on a finished machine.
myths.a4: She imagined manipulating symbols beyond ordinary arithmetic, provided their relationships could be expressed as rules. Note A mentions the possibility of composing music.
myths.q5: Her B7 is today’s seventh Bernoulli number.
myths.a5: Historical B7 in Note G corresponds to modern B8 = -1/30. Modern B7 is zero. Always check the notation when reading old formulas.
myths.quoteTranslation: Original English wording, retaining the historical spelling “any thing”.
myths.quoteContext: Note G, 1843. She is discussing the Analytical Engine and the instructions we can give it. This quotation alone does not settle debates about modern AI’s capabilities.
myths.fictionLabel: A fictional line for this website
myths.fictionTitle: What our salon puts in her mouth
myths.fictionText: We made up this sentence for fun. It is not a historical Ada Lovelace quotation. Her modern startups and beach coding are fictional too.
making.title: Behind the scenes with AI
making.deck: Real requests, real changes and lessons from this website. Even a digital salon needs an editor, testing and the occasional furniture rearrangement.
making.heading: How ideas became a website
making.intro: This website is a collaboration between Miroslav Reiter, ChatGPT and Codex. Successive requests added humour, new pages, five languages, appearance modes and easier mobile controls.
making.roles: Miroslav defines the purpose and requests specific changes. AI helps with design, writing, translation and code. Historical claims need sources, generated images need labels and the result needs human judgement.
making.promptNote: The examples below are real excerpts from the author’s requests in this chat. We retain the original Slovak wording in every language edition and add a translation or explanation. This is not a complete conversation transcript.
making.humorPrompt: Translation: make the website funny and entertaining.
making.humorResult: Result: historical projects sit alongside TeaScript, a fictional modern CV, a salon advice column and AI beach scenes. Fiction is explicitly labelled.
making.headerPrompt: Translation: put the language and appearance switches next to each other in the header so they take up less space.
making.headerResult: Result: language and appearance controls sit side by side. On mobile, the time machine, cards, advice and newspaper links moved into the menu. New learning pages are under Discover.
making.photoPrompt: Translation: add my photograph from the VITA website to About Ada.
making.photoResult: Result: About Ada contains the original VITA photograph, screen-reader text and a source link. The author’s portrait was not AI-generated.
making.compareText: Real screenshots of earlier Slovak versions show the addition of the author’s photograph. Text inside the screenshots is Slovak; the captions are translated.
making.beforeText: An author card without a photograph.
making.afterText: A VITA photograph with its source.
making.beforeAlt: Earlier Slovak About Ada page showing the author card without a photograph
making.afterAlt: Slovak About Ada page after adding Miroslav Reiter’s photograph
making.lesson1Title: The header took up too much space
making.lesson1: The author requested more compact controls. Shrinking the text was not enough: we put the switches on one row and moved extra mobile links into the menu.
making.lesson2Title: Emoji flags are not dependable everywhere
making.lesson2: The language picker needed flags that displayed on Windows too. We used separate SVG images alongside the language’s name and code.
making.lesson3Title: Visible text must match the accessible name
making.lesson3: Checks led us to adjust the controls’ screen-reader names so they included the visible language code. Good looks alone are not a sufficient usability check.
making.checkText: We check links, translation coverage, mobile layouts, keyboard controls and interactive behaviour. Source files and downloadable materials are kept in GitHub.
making.limits: Automated checks do not replace a complete accessibility audit or expert review of every translation. The website does not claim full WCAG certification. Further updates address specific findings.
